passage: Santiago stood at the foot of the slide ladder and counted under his breath. "One, two, three children in front of me." His sister Rosa watched from the bench. "Why are your lips moving?" "Counting," he whispered. "Three more, then me." A girl went down. "Two more, then me." His foot had stopped tapping. When the last child ran off, he climbed the ladder, sat at the top and pushed himself away.

qa.q: How many children were in front of Santiago at first?
qa.a: There were three children in front of him.

qa.q: What does the stopped tapping of Santiago's foot suggest about how he feels while waiting?
qa.a: It suggests he feels calmer and less impatient. Knowing his place in the line makes the wait easier to bear.

qa.q: What could Santiago do if the line stopped moving, and why?
qa.a: He could ask Rosa or another grown-up to check what is holding it up. An adult can settle a stuck line quickly.

qa.q: How does the waiting look to Rosa?
qa.a: Rosa sees her brother's lips moving and does not know why until he says. She sees him waiting patiently without a fuss.

grounding: A child counts the children ahead at the slide and works out how many turns come before their own.
